deep.reconstruction:
PURPOSE. Gauss reduces comparison stars a, b, c, d for his 1815 Juno observations. The next page is headed 'Reduction der Junobeobachtungen'. The stars come from a Lalande zone of 21 April 1796 (Histoire Céleste). They are brought to apparent places for 29 March 1815, using Piazzi stars and one Mayer star (534 M.) as references.

(A) RAW LALANDE DATA → TRUE 1796 VALUES. Each row gives a transit time T and an apparent zenith-distance-like quantity z. These are followed by a correction ΔT (≈ −30.6 s) and a correction Δz (≈ +61″).
- The side table supplies Δz and ΔT for z = 46°, 47°, 48°:
  - Δz = 58.70, 60.74, 62.88; ΔT = −30.90, −30.70, −30.50.
- Δz is refraction. The logs 1.78032, 1.79518, 1.81023 (= 60.30″, 62.40″, 64.60″) equal ≈ 58.2″·tan z.
- These are multiplied by a meteorological factor:
  - thermometer 14.2 gives log 9.98740;
  - barometer 28.16 gives log 0.00088;
  - total log factor 9.98828 (×0.9734).
- Example: 10^(1.79518−0.01172) = 60.74.
- Δz and ΔT are linearly interpolated in z. For a, z = 47°21′17″ gives Δz = 61.49″ and ΔT = −30.63 s.
- Results:
  - a: 12h48m23.87s, 47°22′18.49″
  - b: 12h49m39.78s, 47°26′18.63″
  - Pia.* I: 12h51m6.80s, 46°13′37.13″
  - c: 12h51m38.17s, 47°20′37.43″
  - d: 12h51m53.04s, 47°11′38.12″
  - Pia.* II: 12h54m20.74s, 47°27′4.66″
  - 534 M.: 13h3m35.07s, 46°18′23.29″

(B) CALIBRATION AGAINST CATALOGUE STARS. For the three reference stars Gauss forms two quantities.
- Corr AR = catalogue RA (computed below, reduced to the 1796 apparent place) minus Lalande RA: −0.12 s, −0.36 s, +0.35 s; mean −0.04 s.
- The constant z + δ = 48°50′56.27″, 55.84″, 60.27″; mean 48°50′57.46″. This is the Paris latitude plus an instrumental zero-point.
- Hence for a programme star: δ = 48°50′57.46″ − z_true and α = T − 0.04 s.

(C) CATALOGUE STARS 1800 → APPARENT 21 Apr 1796. Notation: t = −3.696 yr, log 3.696 = 0.56773.
- Precession in α: m′ = m + n sinα tanδ (tabulated logs 1.66124, 1.66210, 1.65820). Applied amounts: −2′49.42″, −2′49.76″, −2′48.24″.
- Precession in δ: n cosα (logs 1.29137, 1.29003, 1.28443). Applied amounts: +1′12.28″, +1′12.07″, +1′11.15″.
- Aberration and nutation for ⊙ = 1s2°28′ and Ω = 3s14°42′ are computed with auxiliary angles. Here ⊙′ = 34°45′ is the Sun's right ascension (tan ⊙′ = tan⊙ / cosε), and ☊′ = 109°25′ is a nutation auxiliary angle.
  - Aberration in α: A cos(α−⊙′) secδ, with log A = 1.2805n, i.e. A = −20.25·√((cos⊙ cosε)² + sin²⊙) = −19.07. Values +17.71, +17.79, +18.07.
  - Aberration in δ, part ∝ sinδ: A sin(⊙′−α) sinδ, giving +0.33, +0.17, +0.27.
  - Aberration in δ, star-independent part: −k sinε cos⊙ cosδ = −6.79. For star I it is written as two bracketed pieces, −3.50 and −3.29.
  - Nutation in α, star-independent part: Δψ cosε = −16.00.
  - Nutation in α, star-dependent part: C cos(α−☊′) tanδ with log C = 0.8673n. Values −0.04, −0.02, −0.02.
  - Nutation in δ: −C sin(α−☊′), giving +7.32, +7.33, +7.35.
- Apparent 1796 places:
  - I: 192°46′40.25″ = 12h51m6.68s, δ = +2°37′19.14″
  - II: 193°35′5.71″ = 12h54m20.38s, δ = +1°23′51.18″
  - III: 195°53′51.31″ = 13h3m35.42s, δ = +2°32′36.98″

(D) STAR d, 1796 APPARENT → 1815 APPARENT.
- Starting place: α = 192°58′15.60″ (= 12h51m53.04s × 15) and δ = 48°50′57.46″ − 47°11′38.12″ = 1°39′19.34″.
- Remove the 1796 aberration and nutation, recomputed for this star: −17.72, +16.00, +0.02 in α; −0.20, +6.79, −7.32 in δ. Result: mean 1796 place 192°58′13.90″, +1°39′18.61″.
- Precession over t = 1815.244 − 1796.304 = 18.940 yr (log 1.27738), with m = 10^1.66313 = 46.03″ and n = 10^1.30242 = 20.06″:
  - m t = 14′31.98″.
  - n t = 10^2.57980 = 379.9″.
  - cosα gives log 9.98856n; sinα gives log 9.35508n.
  - n t cosα = −6′10.13″.
  - n t sinα tanδ̄ = −2.41″, using the mean declination of the interval (log tan = 8.44701, δ̄ ≈ 1°36′14″).
  - Mean 1815 place: 193°12′43.47″, +1°33′8.48″.
- Apply aberration and nutation for 29 Mar 1815: ⊙ = 0s8°19′, Ω = 3s8°31′, ⊙′ = 9°4′, ☊′ = 95°40′, log A = 1.2699n, log C = 0.8601n.
  - In α: +18.58, −16.36, +0.03.
  - In δ: −0.04, −3.97, −4.00, +7.18. The bracketed −3.97 and −4.00 make up the −7.97 term, −k sinε cos⊙.
- Result: 'd apparens' 193°12′45.72″, +1°33′7.65″.
errors: Probable slip: the RA of d is converted as 12h51m53.04s → 192°58′15.60″ without applying the mean Corr AR of −0.04 s. The next page does apply it for c (38.17 − 0.04 → 192°54′31.95″). So d's 1796 RA, and hence its 1815 apparent RA, is about 0.6″ too large.

Star III (534 M.): the annual RA precession used, log 1.65820 = 45.52″, is smaller than m + n sinα tanδ ≈ 45.81″ computed with the same constants that fit stars I and II. The difference is about 1.1″ over 3.7 yr. This may be deliberate: a catalogue annual variation including proper motion. It cannot be judged from this page alone.

All other additions, log sums and sexagesimal/time conversions on the page check to within 0.01–0.02 units. The precise constants behind ☊′ and C in the nutation could not be reconstructed exactly: they are consistent with a nutation in longitude of about 18.0″ sinΩ, but not fully determined. No error is implied by this.

results.what: Reduction of Lalande's Histoire Céleste zone observations: refraction interpolated in zenith distance with thermometer/barometer factor, plus clock/instrument correction, with zero-points calibrated on Piazzi and Mayer stars (latitude + instrumental constant 48°50′57.46″, Corr AR −0.04 s)
results.modern_name: Reduction of meridian zone observations / differential calibration against catalogue stars
results.usually_credited_to: Standard practice; Lalande's zones were systematically reduced later (Baily's 1847 catalogue; Schumacher's reduction tables of 1825)

results.what: Aberration written as A cos(α−⊙′)secδ and A sin(⊙′−α)sinδ + const·cosδ, with ⊙′ = Sun's right ascension and A = k√(cos²⊙cos²ε + sin²⊙)
results.modern_name: Annual aberration in auxiliary-angle form (precursor of Besselian day numbers)
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss's own aberration/nutation tables (Monatliche Correspondenz 1808); Bessel's Tabulae Regiomontanae (1830) for day numbers

results.what: Nutation in α and δ as Δψ cosε + C cos(α−☊′)tanδ and −C sin(α−☊′) with an auxiliary angle ☊′
Precession over 18.94 yr in α and δ using m, n with the mean declination of the interval in the n sinα tanδ term
results.modern_name: Precession in right ascension and declination (mid-epoch approximation)

deep.surprise_reason: Routine observational-astronomy reduction work: Lalande stars reduced to apparent places for comparison with Juno in 1815. The method is Gauss's own published aberration/nutation table formalism. Mildly interesting as evidence that Gauss used Lalande's zones with Piazzi calibration in 1815, decades before Baily's reduction, but not mathematically novel.

transcription_corrections: Pia.* (first) row: the refraction correction is +59.13, not +59.17 (image and the result 46.13.37.13 agree).
The '2.37' beside ⊙ = 1.2.28 is the declination argument (δ ≈ 2°37′) of star I, paired with α = 192.47 as table arguments; it is not part of the Sun's longitude.
Star I decl. corrections: −3.50 and −3.29 are bracketed together, forming the constant aberration term −6.79.
In the d block the second 1815 decl. entry is a crossed-out value replaced by '+1.33.8.48'. The 1815 decl. corrections are −0.04, then bracketed −3.97 and −4.00, then +7.18.
Under star I's log columns, '9,0626' is a struck/smudged repetition, not a result.
Column order of logs: aberration AR, aberration decl (sinδ part), nutation AR (tanδ part), nutation decl; the last row gives the logs of the resulting corrections.
